provenance: Original course figures generated from canonical formulas; no downloaded third-party artwork.

figures.title: One integral, different measures
figures.alt: For h(x)=x on [0,1], equal endpoint atoms and uniform length each give integral one-half; a half atom at zero plus half uniform mass gives one-quarter. Arrows denote point mass; shaded area denotes continuous mass.

figures.title: Monotone convergence illustrated
figures.alt: On [0,1], u_n(x)=(1-2^(-n))x increases pointwise to x. Curves for n=1,2,4 lie below x. Exact integrals increase from one-quarter toward one-half. This finite illustration does not prove the theorem.

figures.title: Dominated convergence illustrated
figures.alt: The curves x^n/(1+x) for n=1,2,4,8 share the integrable envelope g=1 on [0,1]. The pointwise limit is zero for x<1 and one-half at x=1. The exceptional singleton has measure zero and the limiting integral is zero.

figures.title: Radon–Nikodym reweighting
figures.alt: Finite reference masses (1,2,3) become (2,1,6) under multipliers (2,1/2,2). On [0,1] with length reference, r(x)=2x assigns mass three-quarters to [1/2,1], whose reference mass is one-half.

figures.title: Mixed Radon–Nikodym derivative
figures.alt: For rho equal to length plus counting measure on nonnegative integers, display [0,1]: the reference has endpoint atoms of mass one and continuous density one. The weight is one-half at zero and between endpoints but zero at one. The target has a half atom at zero plus half uniform mass and no atom at one. Atomic mass and continuous density use separate rows.

figures.title: Circle law and the choice of reference
figures.alt: A uniform-angle law has all its probability on the unit circle, a set of zero plane area, so it has no density against area. Against arc-length measure on the circle its density is 1/(2 pi); a quarter-circle arc has probability one-quarter.
